title: JPA, database migrations, and transactions — Java Practice
description: Independent practice: Persist the expense API safely under concurrent updates. Seven questions with explanations.
author: DailyCoder

questions.prompt: Why not make every relationship eager to solve query issues?

options.text: All entities must have no relationships
It can fetch unnecessary data and create other query costs

questions.explanation: Choose a deliberate fetch plan for each use case.

questions.prompt: Does self-invocation normally trigger a new proxy-based @Transactional interception?
questions.explanation: A direct internal call bypasses the proxy interception.

options.text: Deleting all tables on every startup

questions.prompt: What should happen to an optimistic-lock conflict?

options.text: Surface or handle it according to the operation’s contract

questions.explanation: The caller needs a deliberate conflict policy.

questions.prompt: Should database integration tests use the production database family?

options.text: Only if there are no migrations
No, every SQL dialect is identical

questions.explanation: Dialect and transaction differences can matter.

questions.prompt: Does @Transactional imply the strongest isolation level automatically?
questions.explanation: Isolation depends on transaction configuration and database defaults.

options.text: Concurrent update with a stale version → optimistic-lock failure
Both writes always succeed and the later write silently wins
The version column is ignored because it is a Long
Every read is rejected before any update

questions.explanation: Two transactions load the same row and version. One transaction updates the row and increments the version. The stale version no longer matches, so the second update fails.
